1.4: Factorial: the product of all positive integers from 1 to n, written n! = n(n−1)(n−2)…3·2·1; by definition 0! = 1. Example: 5! = 120.
Permutation: an ordered arrangement of r objects chosen from n distinct objects; the number is ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n−r)!. Example: ⁵P₂ = 20 (AB and BA are different).
Combination: a selection of r objects from n without regard to order; ⁿCᵣ = n!/[r!(n−r)!]. Example: ⁵C₂ = 10 (AB and BA are the same). Note ⁿPᵣ = r!·ⁿCᵣ.
1.6: (i) Permutations of 2 letters from A, B, C, D: ⁴P₂ = 4!/2! = 12 — AB, BA, AC, CA, AD, DA, BC, CB, BD, DB, CD, DC.
(ii) Combinations: ⁴C₂ = 4!/(2!·2!) = 6 — AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD.
1.11: Probability is a numerical measure of the chance (likelihood) that an event will occur. It lies between 0 and 1: 0 means the event is impossible and 1 means it is certain.
Classical definition: if an experiment has n equally likely, mutually exclusive outcomes and m of them favour event A, then P(A) = m/n.

Relative-frequency definition: if an experiment is repeated n times and A occurs m times, P(A) = lim (m/n) as n → ∞. Probability is used in gambling, insurance, business decisions, quality control and science.
1.12: (i) Random experiment — an experiment whose outcome cannot be predicted in advance, though all possible outcomes are known (tossing a coin).
(ii) Sample space — the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, S = {H, T}. (iii) Outcomes — the individual results of the experiment (sample points).
(iv) Event — any subset of the sample space, e.g. getting an even number when a die is rolled = {2, 4, 6}.
(v) Impossible event — an event that cannot occur, the empty set φ, P = 0 (getting 7 on a die). (vi) Sure event — an event that always occurs, the whole sample space S, P = 1.
1.13: (i) Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together in a single trial (A∩B = φ), so P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B); not mutually exclusive events can occur together, so P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B).

(ii) Independent events: the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other, P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B); dependent events: the occurrence of one changes the probability of the other, P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B/A).

(iii) Probability P(A) is measured on the whole sample space; conditional probability P(A/B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) is the probability of A when it is known that B has occurred (the sample space is reduced to B).
1.14: Equally likely events — events that have the same chance of occurring, e.g. head and tail of a fair coin.
Compound events — events consisting of two or more sample points, e.g. getting an odd number on a die {1, 3, 5}.
Exhaustive events — events whose union is the whole sample space, so that at least one of them must occur, e.g. {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5, 6} when a die is rolled.
1.21: (a) Addition law for not mutually exclusive events: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). Proof: A∪B = A ∪ (Ā∩B), where A and Ā∩B are mutually exclusive, so P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(Ā∩B). Also B = (A∩B) ∪ (Ā∩B), so P(Ā∩B) = P(B) − P(A∩B). Substituting gives the result.
1.23: Multiplication law for independent events: if A and B are independent, P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B). Proof (classical): if A can occur in m₁ of n₁ ways and B in m₂ of n₂ ways independently, then both occur in m₁m₂ of n₁n₂ ways, so P(A∩B) = (m₁m₂)/(n₁n₂) = P(A)P(B).
Multiplication law for dependent events: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B/A) = P(B)·P(A/B). Proof: by definition P(B/A) = P(A∩B)/P(A), so P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B/A).
1.26: (a) Conditional probability is the probability of an event A when it is known that another event B has already occurred: P(A/B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), P(B) > 0.
2.4: A random variable is a function (rule) that assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment; its value depends on chance.
Examples: the number of heads when three coins are tossed (0, 1, 2, 3); the sum of dots on two dice (2 to 12); the height of a randomly selected student; the number of defective items in a lot.
2.5: Discrete random variable — takes a finite or countable number of separate values, usually counts: number of heads, number of children in a family, number of accidents per day.
Continuous random variable — can take any value in an interval, usually measurements: height, weight, temperature, time taken to finish a task.
2.7: Probability distribution: a table, graph or formula giving all possible values of a random variable together with their probabilities.

Probability function (p.m.f.) f(x) = P(X = x) for a discrete random variable; probability density function (p.d.f.) f(x) for a continuous random variable, where probabilities are areas under f(x): P(a < X < b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx.
Two basic properties: (1) f(x) ≥ 0 for all x; (2) Σ f(x) = 1 (discrete) or ∫ f(x)dx = 1 over the whole range (continuous).
2.8: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}; X = number of heads.
2.9: S = {BBB, BBG, BGB, GBB, BGG, GBG, GGB, GGG} (8 equally likely outcomes); X = number of girls.
2.11: X = (number of heads) − (number of tails) for 3 tosses: TTT → −3; one head → 1 − 2 = −1; two heads → 2 − 1 = 1; HHH → 3.
2.12: 36 equally likely outcomes; X = |difference of dots|.
2.16: Mathematical expectation E(X) is the long-run average (mean) value of a random variable: E(X) = Σ x f(x) for a discrete variable and ∫ x f(x)dx for a continuous one.
Properties: (1) E(a) = a for a constant; (2) E(aX) = aE(X); (3) E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; (4) E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y); (5) E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) when X and Y are independent; (6) Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
3.4: A discrete uniform distribution gives equal probability to each of k possible values x₁, …, x_k: f(x) = 1/k.
Example: the number on a fair die, f(x) = 1/6 for x = 1, …, 6. Mean = (k+1)/2 and variance = (k²−1)/12 for values 1 to k.
3.5: Random digits are the digits 0–9 each occurring with equal probability 1/10, independently of one another.

Random numbers are numbers formed from random digits; a random number generator is a device or computer program (e.g. RAND in a calculator/computer) that produces such numbers; a random number table is a printed table of random digits arranged in rows and columns, used to select random samples.
3.6: Number the colleges from 001 to 206 (three-digit numbers).
Start at any point of the random number table and read three-digit numbers in a fixed direction (row or column).
Select a college whenever the number lies between 001 and 206; ignore numbers above 206 and repetitions; continue until 10 different colleges are selected — these form the random sample.
3.7: i) Bernoulli experiment — a trial with only two possible outcomes, success or failure, with P(success) = p.
ii) Bernoulli random variable — X = 1 for success and 0 for failure.
iii) Binomial experiment — n independent Bernoulli trials with the same probability of success p.
iv) Binomial random variable — X = number of successes in n trials, X = 0, 1, …, n.
3.8: Bernoulli distribution: f(x) = pˣq¹⁻ˣ, x = 0, 1, where q = 1 − p.
Mean E(X) = 0·q + 1·p = p; E(X²) = p, so variance = p − p² = pq; standard deviation = √(pq).
3.9: i) A binomial experiment consists of n repeated trials with conditions: (1) fixed number of trials n; (2) each trial has two outcomes, success and failure; (3) probability of success p is constant; (4) trials are independent.
ii) For X ~ b(n, p), f(x) = ⁿCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ. Mean = Σ x f(x) = np (taking np out and summing the remaining binomial terms to 1); E[X(X−1)] = n(n−1)p², so variance = n(n−1)p² + np − n²p² = npq.
3.18: a) A binomial distribution gives the probability of x successes in n independent trials each with success probability p: f(x) = ⁿCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ, x = 0, 1, …, n. It arises in practice whenever a fixed number of independent two-outcome trials is made — e.g. number of defective items in a sample, number of heads in coin tosses, number of patients cured.
b) Mean = np and S.D = √(npq) (derived by E(X) = np and E[X(X−1)] = n(n−1)p², giving variance npq).
3.29: For a hypergeometric distribution (n items drawn without replacement from N items of which k are successes): f(x) = ᵏCₓ·ᴺ⁻ᵏCₙ₋ₓ / ᴺCₙ.
3.30: N = 11 balls, k = 7 black, n = 5 drawn; P(X = x) = ⁷Cₓ·⁴C₅₋ₓ / ¹¹C₅ with ¹¹C₅ = 462; X can be 1 to 5 (there are only 4 white balls).
4.4: (a) A continuous random variable X has a uniform (rectangular) distribution on (a, b) if f(x) = 1/(b − a) for a < x < b and 0 otherwise.
(b) Mean = ∫ₐᵇ x/(b−a) dx = (a + b)/2; E(X²) = (a² + ab + b²)/3, so variance = (b − a)²/12.
4.5: The normal distribution is a continuous, bell-shaped, symmetric distribution with p.d.f. f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}, −∞ < x < ∞, with parameters μ (mean) and σ (S.D).

Importance: many natural and social measurements (heights, weights, errors, marks) are approximately normal; it is the basis of the central limit theorem — sampling distributions of means are approximately normal; binomial and Poisson distributions approach it; and most tests of significance and confidence intervals are based on it.
4.6: Definition: X is normally distributed with mean μ and variance σ² if f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] e^{−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)}, −∞ < x < ∞.

Properties: bell-shaped and symmetric about μ; mean = median = mode; the tails never touch the x-axis; total area = 1; skewness = 0 and kurtosis (β₂) = 3; Q₁ and Q₃ are equidistant from the mean; M.D ≈ (4/5)σ and Q.D ≈ (2/3)σ; about 68.3%, 95.4% and 99.7% of the area lie within μ ± σ, μ ± 2σ and μ ± 3σ.
4.7: Standard normal variable: Z = (X − μ)/σ, which has mean 0 and S.D 1.
Standard normal distribution: the normal distribution of Z, φ(z) = (1/√(2π)) e^{−z²/2}.

Role: any normal variable can be changed to Z, so one table of areas (Z-table) gives probabilities for all normal distributions; it is also used to compare scores from different distributions and in tests of significance.
4.29: Ordinate method of fitting: (1) find the mean x̄ and S.D σ of the given data (N = 1000); (2) for each class mid-point x compute z = (x − x̄)/σ; (3) find the ordinate φ(z) from the table of normal ordinates; (4) expected frequency = (N·h/σ)·φ(z), where h is the class width; (5) round off and compare with observed frequencies.
4.30: Fit by the same method: compute x̄ and σ of the data, then for each mid-point x find z = (x − x̄)/σ, the ordinate φ(z), and expected frequency = (N·h/σ)·φ(z) (or, by the area method, N × area of each class under the normal curve).
5.4: Population — the whole collection of individuals or items under study (all students of a college).
Sample — a part of the population selected to represent it (100 students).
Sampling — the process of selecting a sample from a population in order to draw conclusions about the population.
5.5: Sampling is needed because it saves time, money and labour; gives results quickly; makes more detailed and accurate study possible with trained staff; is the only method when the population is infinite or when testing destroys items (life of bulbs); and when the population is scattered or not fully accessible. Complete enumeration (census) is costly, slow and sometimes impossible.
5.6: (i) Sampling frame — a complete list of all units of the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g. voters' list).
(ii) Sample design — the plan for selecting the sample: the method of selection, sample size and estimation procedure.
(iii) Survey — a method of collecting information from a population or sample, by census or sample survey, through questionnaires, interviews or observation.
5.7: (i) A finite population has a fixed, countable number of units (students of a class); an infinite population has an unlimited number (stars, tosses of a coin).

(ii) In sampling with replacement each selected unit is returned before the next draw, so a unit can be selected more than once and draws are independent; without replacement a unit can appear only once and draws are dependent.

(iii) Sampling error is the difference between a sample estimate and the population parameter due to studying only a part of the population; non-sampling errors arise from mistakes in collection, recording, processing, non-response or bias and occur in both census and samples.
5.9: (a) Objectives of sampling: to obtain information about the population at less cost and time; to estimate population parameters; to test hypotheses about the population; and to measure the reliability of estimates.

(b) Parameter — a numerical value describing the population (μ, σ, P); statistic — a value computed from a sample (x̄, s, p̂); estimator — a statistic (rule/formula) used to estimate a parameter, e.g. x̄ for μ.
5.10: Sampling errors arise because only a part of the population is studied; they can be reduced by increasing the sample size and using better (e.g. stratified) sampling designs.

Non-sampling errors arise from faulty questionnaires, wrong or missing responses, interviewer bias, recording and processing mistakes; they are reduced by careful planning, training of staff, pre-testing questionnaires, follow-up of non-respondents and careful checking of data.
5.11: Probability (random) sampling: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection; selection is by chance; results can be generalised and sampling error measured (simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster sampling).

Non-probability sampling: selection depends on the judgement or convenience of the investigator; chances are unknown; results may be biased and error cannot be measured (purposive, quota, convenience sampling).
5.12: (i) Simple random sampling — every unit (and every sample of size n) has an equal chance of selection, using lottery or random number tables.
(ii) Stratified random sampling — the population is divided into homogeneous groups (strata) and a random sample is taken from each stratum, often in proportion to its size.
(iii) Systematic random sampling — units are arranged in order; the first unit is selected at random from the first k units (k = N/n) and then every kth unit is taken.
5.13: A simple random sample is one in which every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
(i) Goldfish bowl (lottery) method: write the number of each unit on identical slips, put them in a bowl, mix thoroughly and draw n slips one by one.

(ii) Random number table method: number the units, read numbers of the required digits from a random number table, and select the units whose numbers appear, ignoring numbers outside the range and repeats (without replacement).
5.14: (i) Random sample — every unit has a known (equal) chance of selection.
(ii) Non-random sample — units are chosen by judgement or convenience, not by chance.
(iii) Stratified random sample — random samples taken from each homogeneous sub-group (stratum) of the population.
(iv) Systematic random sample — every kth unit taken after a random start.
5.15: From any random starting point in the random number table read three-digit numbers; select a city if its number is between 001 and 200, skipping larger numbers and repeats.
Example (random start, reading down a column): 128, 057, 193, 004, 162, 079, 145, 031, 110, 186 → these 10 cities form the sample. (The actual numbers depend on the table used.)
5.16: (a) Proportional allocation: nᵢ = n·Nᵢ/N for each stratum.
5.18: (i) Sampling distribution — the probability distribution of a statistic (e.g. x̄) obtained from all possible samples of the same size from a population.
(ii) Standard error — the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic, e.g. σ_x̄ = σ/√n.
(iii) Finite population correction (fpc) — the factor √[(N − n)/(N − 1)] used in the standard error when sampling without replacement from a finite population; it is ignored when n < 5% of N.
5.25: The sampling distribution of x̄₁ − x̄₂ is the distribution of the differences of means of all possible pairs of independent samples of sizes n₁ and n₂ from two populations.
Properties: mean μ_{x̄₁−x̄₂} = μ₁ − μ₂; standard error σ_{x̄₁−x̄₂} = √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂); it is normal if the populations are normal and approximately normal for large samples.
5.28: Sample proportion p̂ = X/n, the fraction of units in a sample having a characteristic.

The sampling distribution of p̂ is its distribution over all possible samples of size n. Properties: mean μ_p̂ = P; standard error σ_p̂ = √(PQ/n) (with fpc √[(N−n)/(N−1)] for finite populations without replacement); approximately normal for large n.
6.4: Estimation is the process of using sample data to obtain values (point or interval) for unknown population parameters.
An estimator is the rule, formula or statistic used to estimate a parameter (x̄ = Σx/n); an estimate is the numerical value obtained by applying the estimator to a particular sample (x̄ = 52.4).
6.5: i) Statistical inference — drawing conclusions about a population from sample information; its two branches are estimation and testing of hypotheses.

ii) Types of estimates — point estimate: a single value used as the estimate of the parameter (x̄ = 50); interval estimate: a range of values with a stated confidence that it contains the parameter (48 < μ < 52 with 95% confidence).
6.6: i) A point estimate is a single number used as the estimate of a parameter; an interval estimate is a range (L, U) together with a confidence level that it contains the parameter.
ii) An estimator is the formula or statistic (a random variable); an estimate is the particular value of the estimator obtained from a given sample.
6.7: i) Unbiasedness — an estimator T is unbiased for θ if E(T) = θ; e.g. x̄ is unbiased for μ and s² = Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1) is unbiased for σ².
ii) Efficiency — of two unbiased estimators, the one with smaller variance is more efficient; e.g. for a normal population the mean is more efficient than the median.
iii) Consistency — T is consistent if it approaches θ as n increases (its variance tends to 0); x̄ is consistent for μ.
iv) Sufficiency — T is sufficient if it uses all the information in the sample about θ; Σx (or x̄) is sufficient for μ.
6.8: Bias is the difference between the expected value of an estimator and the true value of the parameter: Bias = E(T) − θ.

Factors introducing bias: faulty sampling methods (non-random selection), an incomplete or outdated sampling frame, non-response, wrong questions or interviewer influence, deliberate wrong answers, faulty measuring instruments and wrong formulas of estimation.
6.11: E(T₁) = (μ + 2μ + μ)/4 = μ and E(T₂) = (μ + μ + μ)/3 = μ, so both T₁ and T₂ are unbiased.
Since Var(T₂) < Var(T₁), T₂ (the sample mean) is the more efficient estimator.
6.12: Confidence interval estimation gives a range of values (L, U), computed from sample data, that is expected to contain the unknown parameter with a stated probability (confidence level 1 − α), e.g. x̄ ± z_{α/2}·σ/√n for μ.
A 95% confidence interval means that if many samples were taken and intervals made in the same way, about 95% of them would contain the true parameter.
6.13: i) Confidence limits — the lower and upper end points L and U of a confidence interval.
ii) Confidence coefficient — the probability (1 − α) that the interval contains the parameter, e.g. 0.95.
iii) Level of significance (α) — the probability that the interval does not contain the parameter (risk of error), e.g. 0.05.
iv) Precision of a confidence interval — measured by its width; a narrower interval is more precise (precision increases with larger n and smaller σ).
6.22: The t-distribution is used instead of Z when the population standard deviation σ is unknown and is estimated by s, and the sample size is small (n < 30), the population being approximately normal.
Then the interval is x̄ ± t_{α/2,(n−1)}·s/√n; for large samples Z can be used even when σ is unknown.
7.4: Hypothesis — an assumption or statement about something that may be true or false.
Statistical hypothesis — a statement about a population parameter or the form of a distribution, e.g. H₀: μ = 50.
Testing of hypothesis — the procedure of deciding, on the basis of sample data, whether to reject or not reject a statistical hypothesis.
7.5: (i) Hypothesis testing decides whether a claim about a parameter is supported by sample evidence; (ii) estimation finds the (point or interval) value of an unknown parameter from a sample.

Principal steps of testing: (1) state H₀ and H₁; (2) choose the level of significance α; (3) select the test statistic (Z, t, χ², F); (4) find the critical (rejection) region; (5) compute the test statistic from the sample; (6) decide: reject H₀ if the value falls in the critical region, otherwise do not reject; (7) state the conclusion.
7.6: (i) Null hypothesis H₀ is the statement being tested, usually of no difference (μ = μ₀); alternative hypothesis H₁ is accepted when H₀ is rejected (μ ≠ μ₀, μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀).
(ii) A simple hypothesis specifies the distribution completely (μ = 50 with σ known); a composite hypothesis does not (μ > 50).
(iii) Type-I error: rejecting a true H₀ (probability α); Type-II error: accepting a false H₀ (probability β).
(iv) Acceptance region: values of the test statistic for which H₀ is not rejected; rejection (critical) region: values for which H₀ is rejected.
7.7: (a) Level of significance α — the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (Type-I error), usually 5% or 1%.

(b) Test statistic — a statistic computed from the sample whose distribution under H₀ is known (Z, t, χ², F); a test of significance is the procedure that uses it to decide whether the observed difference is significant or due to chance.
(c) A small sample usually has n < 30 (exact tests like t are used); a large sample has n ≥ 30 (normal approximation, Z-test, can be used).
7.8: A one-sided (one-tailed) test has the critical region in one tail of the sampling distribution, used when H₁ is directional (H₁: μ > μ₀ — right tail, or μ < μ₀ — left tail).
A two-sided (two-tailed) test has critical regions in both tails, each of area α/2, used when H₁: μ ≠ μ₀.
Diagram: draw the normal curve; for a right-tailed test shade the area α beyond +z_α; for a two-tailed test shade α/2 beyond −z_{α/2} and +z_{α/2}.
7.9: Testing H₀: μ = μ₀ when σ is known (normal population): (1) H₀: μ = μ₀ against H₁: μ ≠ μ₀ (or > / <); (2) choose α; (3) test statistic Z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n); (4) critical region |Z| ≥ z_{α/2} (or Z ≥ z_α / Z ≤ −z_α); (5) compute Z from the sample; (6) reject H₀ if Z falls in the critical region, otherwise accept; (7) conclusion.
7.15: When σ is unknown and n is small: (1) H₀: μ = μ₀, H₁: μ ≠ μ₀; (2) α; (3) test statistic t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom, s = √[Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)]; (4) critical region |t| ≥ t_{α/2,(n−1)}; (5) compute t; (6) decide and conclude.
7.18: Testing H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ when σ₁ and σ₂ are known: (1) H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0, H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0; (2) α; (3) Z = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/√(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂); (4) critical region |Z| ≥ z_{α/2}; (5) compute; (6) decide and conclude.
7.21: When σ₁ = σ₂ = σ is unknown and samples are small: (1) H₀: μ₁ = μ₂, H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂; (2) α; (3) t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/[s_p√(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)] with pooled s_p² = [(n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²]/(n₁ + n₂ − 2) and n₁ + n₂ − 2 d.f.; (4) critical region |t| ≥ t_{α/2}; (5) compute; (6) decide and conclude.
7.24: For a large sample: (1) H₀: P = P₀, H₁: P ≠ P₀ (or > / <); (2) α; (3) Z = (p̂ − P₀)/√(P₀Q₀/n); (4) critical region |Z| ≥ z_{α/2}; (5) compute Z; (6) reject H₀ if in the critical region; (7) conclusion.
7.28: For large samples: (1) H₀: P₁ = P₂, H₁: P₁ ≠ P₂; (2) α; (3) Z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√[p̂q̂(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)] with pooled p̂ = (x₁ + x₂)/(n₁ + n₂), q̂ = 1 − p̂; (4) critical region |Z| ≥ z_{α/2}; (5) compute; (6) decide and conclude.
8.4: An attribute is a qualitative characteristic that cannot be measured numerically but only noted as present or absent (blindness, literacy, honesty, gender).

Classification: by dichotomy (simple classification) — into two classes, possessing (A) and not possessing (α) the attribute; and manifold classification — into more than two classes (e.g. eye colour: blue, grey, brown); two-way classification uses two attributes at a time (contingency table).
8.5: i. Class symbol — a letter (A, B, α, β, AB, …) denoting a class; class frequency — the number of observations in that class, written in brackets, e.g. (A), (AB).
ii. Positive classes contain attributes A, B (presence); negative classes α, β (absence).
iii. Order of classes — the number of attributes specified: N is of order 0; (A), (α) of order 1; (AB), (Aβ) of order 2; and so on.
iv. Ultimate class frequencies — frequencies of the highest order, e.g. (AB), (Aβ), (αB), (αβ) for two attributes; all other frequencies can be found from them.
8.6: i. Two-way classification — classification of data by two attributes at the same time, giving a 2 × 2 (or r × c) table.
ii. Association of attributes — the tendency of two attributes to occur together more (or less) often than expected by chance.
iv. Criterion of independence: A and B are independent if (AB) = (A)(B)/N, i.e. (AB)(αβ) = (Aβ)(αB).
v. Yule's coefficient of association Q = [(AB)(αβ) − (Aβ)(αB)]/[(AB)(αβ) + (Aβ)(αB)], ranging from −1 to +1.
8.7: Association measures the relationship between attributes (qualitative characteristics), using class frequencies and coefficients like Yule's Q or contingency coefficient.
Correlation measures the relationship between variables (quantitative, measurable) using actual values, with Karl Pearson's r ranging from −1 to +1.
8.17: i. Manifold classification — classification of data according to an attribute into more than two classes (e.g. A₁, A₂, …, A_r).
ii. (r × c) contingency table — a two-way table with r rows (classes of one attribute) and c columns (classes of the other), whose cells show observed frequencies.

iii. Chi-square distribution — the distribution of χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E, a continuous, positively skewed distribution from 0 to ∞ with parameter ν (degrees of freedom), used to test independence of attributes and goodness of fit.
8.21: Coefficient of mean square contingency: φ² = χ²/N; the coefficient of contingency C = √[χ²/(χ² + N)] measures the degree of association in an r × c table; it is 0 for independence and approaches (but never reaches) 1 for strong association; its maximum depends on the table size.
9.4: Design of an experiment is the plan of conducting an experiment: deciding the treatments, the experimental units, the number of replications and the way treatments are allotted to units, and the method of analysis, so that valid and efficient conclusions can be drawn with minimum experimental error.
9.5: i. Experimental material — the material on which the experiment is performed (land, animals, plants, patients).
ii. Experimental unit — the smallest division of the material to which a treatment is applied (a plot, an animal).
iii. Treatment — the factor or method whose effect is studied (fertiliser, variety, drug).
iv. Uniformity trial — an experiment in which the same treatment is applied to all units to study the natural variability of the material.
v. Block — a group of homogeneous experimental units.
9.6: Randomization — allotting treatments to experimental units by a random process so that each unit has an equal chance; it removes bias and makes the error estimate valid.
Replication — repeating each treatment on more than one unit; it gives an estimate of experimental error and increases precision.
Local control — grouping homogeneous units into blocks so that variation between blocks is removed from the error, making the design more efficient.
9.7: i. Experimental design is the plan for conducting an experiment — choice of treatments, units, replication and allocation — to obtain valid conclusions with minimum error.
ii. Basic principles: randomization, replication and local control.
9.8: (a) Extraneous factors — factors other than the treatments that may affect the response (soil fertility, temperature, age of animals); they should be controlled.
(b) Experimental error — the variation among units receiving the same treatment, caused by extraneous factors and uncontrolled variation; it is estimated through replication.
9.9: Planning is needed so that the experiment answers the questions asked, with minimum cost, time and effort; it ensures that treatments are compared fairly, experimental error is estimated and reduced, bias is avoided by randomization, and the data can be analysed correctly (by ANOVA) to draw reliable conclusions.
9.10: A completely randomized design (CRD) is one in which treatments are allotted to experimental units completely at random; it is used when units are homogeneous.
Merits: simple to plan and analyse; any number of treatments and replications can be used; maximum error degrees of freedom; missing observations cause no serious problem.
Demerits: suitable only for homogeneous material; less efficient when units vary, because all variation goes into the error.
9.11: Treatments A, B, C, each replicated 5 times on 15 plots.
Number the plots 1 to 15. Using a random number table (or lottery), select 5 plots for treatment A, then 5 of the remaining for B, and the last 5 get C.
Example layout (plot: treatment): 1-B, 2-A, 3-C, 4-A, 5-B, 6-C, 7-C, 8-A, 9-B, 10-A, 11-C, 12-B, 13-A, 14-C, 15-B. ANOVA: total d.f. 14, treatments 2, error 12.
9.12: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is a technique, developed by R. A. Fisher, for splitting the total variation in data into components due to different sources (treatments and error) and testing, by an F-test, whether several population means are equal. The F ratio = MS(treatments)/MS(error) is compared with the table value.
9.13: ANOVA is the method of partitioning total variation into variation between groups (treatments) and within groups (error) to test the equality of several means.
Assumptions: (1) observations are independent and random; (2) each population is normally distributed; (3) the populations have equal variances (homogeneity); (4) effects are additive.
9.14: i. Variance among samples (between treatments) — variation of sample means about the grand mean, SS_B = Σ nᵢ(x̄ᵢ − x̄)².
ii. Variance within samples (error) — variation of observations about their own sample means, SS_W = ΣΣ(xᵢⱼ − x̄ᵢ)².
iii. Total variation — variation of all observations about the grand mean, SS_T = ΣΣ(xᵢⱼ − x̄)² = SS_B + SS_W.
9.15: ANOVA: Treatments d.f. 2, MS = 4; Error d.f. 9, MS = 14.44; F = 4/14.44 = 0.28.
F₀.₀₅(2, 9) = 4.26; since 0.28 < 4.26, H₀ is not rejected — the three population means can be taken as equal.
3.28: Hypergeometric experiment — n items are drawn without replacement from a finite population of N items of which k are 'successes' and N − k 'failures'; the trials are dependent.
Hypergeometric random variable — X = number of successes among the n items drawn.
Hypergeometric probability distribution — P(X = x) = ᵏCₓ·ᴺ⁻ᵏCₙ₋ₓ / ᴺCₙ, x = max(0, n−N+k), …, min(n, k); mean nk/N and variance n(k/N)(1 − k/N)(N − n)/(N − 1).
